flashcards.q: What's the core difference between an open-model and closed-model load test?
flashcards.a: Open model: requests arrive at a rate independent of response time (Poisson/exponential inter-arrival) -- a slow system causes queue buildup, like real public traffic. Closed model: a fixed number of virtual users loop request-wait-repeat, so a slow system just drops each user's effective request rate, hiding the queueing failure mode.

flashcards.q: Why is skipping think time (issuing the next request immediately after the previous response) a common load-testing mistake?
flashcards.a: It massively overstates each virtual user's real request rate -- a user who really issues one request per several seconds gets modeled as issuing requests as fast as the network allows, requiring far fewer VUs to hit a target throughput than reality, and testing a different concurrency scenario than production.

flashcards.q: What distribution best models real user think time, and why not a fixed sleep()?
flashcards.a: Log-normal (right-skewed): most users pause a typical amount, with a long tail of much slower users. A fixed, uniform sleep() smooths out the burst/lull pattern real traffic has and understates the tail.

flashcards.q: Why should you never run real JMeter load generation in GUI mode?
flashcards.a: The GUI's own rendering and listener overhead competes with the load generator for CPU/memory, producing lower achievable throughput and less trustworthy latency numbers. Build the test plan in GUI mode, but execute real runs headless via CLI (jmeter -n -t plan.jmx).

flashcards.q: In k6's ramping-arrival-rate executor, what does it mean if a test run hits maxVUs?
flashcards.a: It's a finding, not just a config limit: it means the system under test can't sustain the target arrival rate without unbounded concurrency/queue growth -- don't just raise maxVUs and rerun without noting why it was hit.

flashcards.q: How does Locust's default concurrency model compare to JMeter's, per a 2026 TestDevLab analysis?
flashcards.a: Locust (gevent-based greenlets) handles roughly 5x more concurrent simulated users than JMeter (which allocates a full thread per virtual user) on identical 8GB hardware.

flashcards.q: Why does Gatling generally achieve the highest throughput per load-generator machine among the open-source tools?
flashcards.a: Its core is built on Netty, using async, non-blocking I/O rather than a thread-per-virtual-user model, which lets one machine sustain more simulated load with less memory/CPU overhead per user.

flashcards.q: Why does testing with identical request payloads/IDs on every virtual user produce misleading cache-hit-rate results?
flashcards.a: Identical payloads give the cache an artificially easy workload (near-100% hit rate), hiding real cache-miss latency. Real traffic has a much wider, typically Zipfian-skewed access distribution across items that should be sampled to reproduce realistic cache behavior.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a step-function ramp and a gradual ramp in load testing, and why run both?
flashcards.a: A step function (instant jump to target load) stresses sudden connection/TLS-handshake bursts and cold caches -- tests burst survival. A gradual ramp tests organic-growth degradation (resource exhaustion, slow-reacting autoscaling). They catch different failure modes, so running only one misses the other.

flashcards.q: What does k6 2.0 (2026) add for AI/CI integration?
flashcards.a: k6 x agent, a command for bootstrapping agentic testing workflows in AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor), plus a new JSON summary output aimed at making end-of-test results easier for CI/CD systems and AI agents to consume.
